Jim

messages.subject: Introduction of Camelot
messages.subject_clean: Introduction of Camelot
messages.body_plain:
Camelot is an open-source, web-based tool to help wildlife conservationists with camera trapping.
Camera Trapping software for Species Identification & Reports.
By Christopher Mann of BitPattern.
Developed in consultation with Fauna & Flora International.

The latest version of Camelot is: 1.0.0
Camelot:

Makes classifying camera trap photos quick and easy
Keeps track of camera trap, camera and species data
Gives you a head start on data analysis
Plays nicely with other software, such as CamtrapR.
Lets multiple people use it at the same time
Runs on Windows, OSX and Linux
Is easy to start using

The Camelot application, source code and documentation are available from https://gitlab.com/camelot-project/camelot

The Camelot community for questions, support and discussion is located at the Google Group https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/camelot-project

Chris and I will be monitoring the Google Group for questions, concerns, comments.

I'd like to thank Chris Mann for his tireless volunteer dedication to this software project. The software as-is will be a huge benefit to conservation scientists. I'd like to thank Dr Benjamin Rawson formerly of FFI-Vietnam (and now of WWF - Greater Mekong) who trusted me with all his images.

And a huge thank you to the FFI Camelot Beta Testers from the Myanmar, Indonesia and Vietnam programs. Your feedback has been invaluable.

Thank you to the moderators and group members for their assistance with understanding unmarked R, and how that fits in to the camera trap software toolbox.

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Issue Running Some Multiple Season Models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachel,
The dynamic occupancy model assumes that sites are closed to changes in occupancy over the survey period. Put another way, we assume that occupancy does not vary within a season. Therefore, you can't model psi as a function of an observation covariate. Your avextemp model says that occupancy varies with some survey-specific temperature -- this is contrary to the fundamental assumption that a site is either occupied or unoccupied in a season. Therefore, you can only model occupancy as a function of static site covariates (things that do not change within a year), for instance "treehab" in your covariate file.

Does this make sense?
Brittany
--
Ph.D. Candidate
Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Conservation Biology
Colorado State University
My website <http://brittany-a-mosher.strikingly.com/> (a work in progress)
brittan...@colostate.edu

messages.subject: Recommendations for elevation as an abundance covariate
messages.subject_clean: Recommendations for elevation as an abundance covariate
messages.body_plain:
In my case the relationship between abundance and elevation isn't linear over the entire sampling range because I sampled beyond the species' elevational limit in one direction (i.e. there are dozens of transects that have no observations because they were at too low an elevation). As I see it, I could:
1. Ignore this and treat elevation as a continuous predictor and get an inaccurate estimate of the relationship between elevation and abundance/density
2. treat elevation as categorical with 'high' and 'low' elevations corresponding to where the species actually occurs, but this would ignore any relationship between elevation and abundance within the elevational range where the species actually occurs.
3. include elevation twice as a categorical and a continuous predictor (potentially with an interaction so that the relationship between abundance and elevation at high elevation isn't impacted too much by the lack of observations at low elevation. I'm assuming that the lack of observations at low elevation are 0's (not NA's) in the linear model relating covariates to expected abundance/density and would therefore still impact the estimate of the relationship between elevation and abundance/density).
4. exclude the sampling data from outside the species' elevational limit (thus I would have a different sample set for each species).
5. Use some form of exponential function.

Any recommendations for when different approaches would be best are appreciated.

messages.subject: Model occupancy from continuous vegetation variables
messages.subject_clean: Model occupancy from continuous vegetation variables
messages.body_plain:
I am new to occupancy modeling and have results, but am not sure I took the correct approach.

I conducted spring bird surveys in cover crop fields and have questions regarding occupancy modeling.

Survey details:
Surveys conducted in 2015 & 2016
Treatments are: corn, corn + cover crop, soybean, soybean + cover crop.
Field were visited roughly 4x each. Each visit, I measured %bare ground, %alive vegetation, %dead vegetation in a 0.5 quadrant. I also
measured Maximum and average height of all vegetation, and density of vegetation (all continuous).

Questions I want to answer with data:
1. Are birds (specie specific) more likely to occupy a field with a cover crop on it?
2. How do vegetation variables influence occupancy of sites?

Question #2:
The way I set this up was by creating 3 sets of models.
(1) The first set was looking at observation covariates (distance of transect, day of year, time after sunrise, etc.) only.
(2) the top model was selected from (1) to include in the next set of models that incorporated the vegetation variables as
observation covariates because they changed each visit.
(3) the top model from (2) was selected and the next set of models incorporated Crop and Year as site covariates.
The top model from (3) is the final model I select.

The results from the models make sense for each specie, but I was told I actually need to average the vegetation variables
to include them on the occupancy side of the equation in order to answer my question. I averaged the vegetation variables for each field
to be able to provide a site covariate, but the results don't make as much sense. I also have to take into account that birds are migrating through and are not necessarily a closed group.

I would like to get clarification on the best approach to my questions and if I did things correct or not. I can provide code if necessary.

Cassandra

messages.body_plain:
If you consider the following suggestion "exploratory" and there aren't too many gasps, you might want to look to see if your observation covariates vary only a little across visits in a season.   Then you might want to consider using the site-season averages for some of those variables for estimating psi and colonization and extinction parameters.  But if for example the temperatures vary among sites due to some factor unrelated to occupancy, then that won't gain you any insight.  (I hope I've put in enough cautionary words.)  I've attached a pdf of the variable "avgintemp" across visits for each site and season.  That variable is (usually) pretty constant across visits.

Jim

Of what you've described,  quadratic or polynomial predictors seem like the best way to fit a more irregular response without being forced to make arguments about how specific categories were delineated and why...to me, at least.

Hello dear all, some time ago I started this topic and I would like to know if there is any criterion to choose among key functions.
Regards
Antonela

El miércoles, 10 de agosto de 2016, 23:18:14 (UTC-3), Jeffrey Royle escribió:

> Dear Antonela,
>
>  1) I think it is ok to use AIC to choose among the key functions if you think this is an important aspect of your problem. Normally I recommend not choosing among detection models because they usually do not correspond to explicit hypotheses. I think the distance sampling community disagrees with me on this point, however.
>
>  2) I do not see the problem with the starting values. Can you produce the exact R code and result?
>
>  3) The null model has only a constant expected density per site and thus the fitted density is indeed constant. I suggest using the ranef() and bup() functions to produce estimates of site-specific abundance. This is discussed in some detail in various parts of the AHM book.  see p 234 and 439 and elsewhere.  I'm sure you can resolve your problem with starting values and produce better site-specific estimates though....

> regards,
> andy

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Re: Nmix.gof.test vs. parboot()
messages.body_plain:
the N-mixture model likelihood is formulated by summing the binomial likelihood for the counts over all possible values of N = max(count):infinity except that we approximate infinity by K, in order to do the summation. So usually K = 50 or 100 or 200 is sufficient to obtain stable MLEs but sometimes , especially for the negative binomial model, the MLEs are very unstable even for very large values of K.

The parboot function is simulating data sets but using the K from the fitted model, and it seems that in your case one of the simulated data sets has an observed count larger than K.   This might be fixed by setting K = 200 or 400 or something but, on the other hand, the likelihood may be unstable and so the problem will persist if that is the case.

messages.subject: Re: Recommendations for elevation as an abundance covariate
messages.subject_clean: Recommendations for elevation as an abundance covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hey Philip,

I agree with John - a ZIP model is a good option for using empirical evidence to define the species ranges, and then model variation in abundance with elevation conditional on presence.  But I'd also say that if you have good a priori evidence, then option #4 where you restrict your abundance estimation to the sites within some predefined range would be acceptable as well.  In fact, it might be good to at least start with this approach and get a feel for what you've got.

I am working with line transects samples in two sites of Patagonia steppe. I intend to estimate density in this two sites, the covariates I am using are topography and  the site.There are no more covs that changes  among sites, as you can see this is a very simple scenario but I think is good for learning. I am new at the unmarked package and I find it very interesting but I need to study a lot.

As the AHM book suggests I tried with the distsamp but when I checked the GOF of the model, the model does not fit, so I  am trying with gdistsamp.

distancia<-transectas_grupos[,2]
transecta<-transectas_grupos[,1]

yDat <- formatDistData(transectas_grupos, distCol="distancia",
                       transectNameCol="transecta", dist.breaks=c(0, 230,440,700))

#transect lenght en metros
tlenght<-c(6000,6600,5900,4500,10200,6500,9900,10000)    #creo el objeto tlenght porque todas las transectas son de
                                                         #distinta longitud

#each site has 500 kmsq sampled

area1<-500
area2<-500

#juntamos las transectas con las covaribales
umf<- unmarkedFrameDS(y=as.matrix(yDat),siteCovs=data.frame(covariables, (area1+area2)),
        dist.breaks=c(0,230,440,700), unitsIn="m",survey="line",
        tlenght,(unitsIn=m))

summary (umf)

hist(umf)
#elijo  Null1 que tiene un ajuste halfnorm  entonces a todos los otros modelos les hago un ajuste halfnorm
NUll1<-distsamp(~1~1, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",unitsOut="kmsq")
SC1<-distsamp(~1~sitio, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",unitsOut="kmsq")
sc2<-distsamp(~1~relieve, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",unitsOut="kmsq")
sc3<-distsamp(~relieve~1, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",unitsOut="kmsq")
sc4<-distsamp(~sitio~1, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",unitsOut="kmsq")
sc5<-distsamp(~sitio~sitio^2, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",unitsOut="kmsq")
sc6<-distsamp(~relieve~relieve, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",unitsOut="kmsq")

#model selection
scs2<-fitList(Null=NUll1,a=SC1,b=sc2,c=sc3,d=sc4,e=sc5,f=sc6 )
ms <- modSel(scs2, nullmod="Null")
ms
NUll1
scs2
# Check out the goodness-of-fit of this model
fm<-c(NUll1,SC1,sc2,sc3,sc4,sc5,sc6)

fitstats <- function(fm) {
  observed <- getY(fm@data)
  expected <- fitted(fm)
  resids <- residuals(fm)
  sse <- sum(resids^2)
  chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected)
  freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2)
  out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)
  return(out)
}
(pb.try2<- parboot(NUll1, fitstats, nsim=1000, report=5))

(c.hat <- pb.try2@t0[2] / mean(pb....@t.star[,2]))

#crate a new unmarked frame
area<-1000
rep<-1
date<-1
hour<-1

umfgDS <- unmarkedFrameGDS(y=as.matrix(yDat),
                           siteCovs=covariables, dist.breaks=c(0,230,440,700),

                           unitsIn="m", survey="line",tlenght, numPrimary=1)

Couple of things I don’t understand:

(1)    You have two sites, but seem to have a total of 8 transects, right ? So, the “site” in the sense of spatial replicate is really the transect. Site is a factor and hence, below, it doesn’t make sense to specify a linear model with site as linear and quadratic effects.

(2)    I am not sure about the role of area1 and area2 as covariates. For site covariates, you need something that varies by the “site” = transect.

(3)    I am also unsure about your specification of the siteCovs. It would be useful to see the result of doing ‘summary(umf)’

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Was this issue resolved? I'm getting some unintuitive results when computing fitted values for a negative binomial N-mixture model that may be related to this. Here's a simple example:

set.seed(45)
yS = matrix(rnbinom(50*5, mu = 1, size = 1), nrow = 50, ncol = 5)
fmNB = pcount(~1~1, data = unmarkedFramePCount(yS), mixture = "NB", K = 500)
fitted(fmNB)[1,1]
[1] 0.0007500683
exp(coef(fmNB)[1]) * plogis(coef(fmNB)[2])
[1] 1.04

Looking at the source the fitted values for the negative binomial mixture seem to be computed using a numerical computation of the means. The K value for this computation is taken as an argument to the 'fitted' function and not from the fitted object. In the example above the default value of K is much too low. Supplying a larger K works better:

fitted(fmNB, K = 500)[1,1]
[1] 1.036696

Jonas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

Thanks for your response! You're right that the data I simulated are standard Poisson. My point was just to try to show what seems to me to be a bug in the 'fitted' function for NB models.

In my example, I would have expected the values from fitted(fmNB) to be equal to exp(coef(fmNB)[1]) * plogis(coef(fmNB)[2]), but that's not the case. This can happen also for data simulated from a proper N-mixture model. In your example 'fitted' gives the correct answer, but if we change lam to e.g. 10 and size to 1/5, fitted(fmNB) is no longer equal to exp(coef(fmNB)[1]) * plogis(coef(fmNB)[2]):

set.seed(45)
nSites  <- 50
nVisits <- 5

lam <- 10
p <- 0.5
N <- rnbinom(50, mu = lam, size = 1/5)

yS <- matrix(rbinom(nSites*nVisits, rep(N,nVisits), p), nrow = nSites, ncol = nVisits)
fmNB <- pcount(~1~1, data = unmarkedFramePCount(yS), mixture = "NB", K = 500)

Now fitted gives:

> fitted(fmNB)[1,1]
[1] 4.144114

but this is not the same as the product of the back transformed coefficients:

> exp(coef(fmNB)[1]) * plogis(coef(fmNB)[2])

lam(Int)
5.647976

Like above, if a larger K is supplied to the fitted function we get a better agreement:

> fitted(fmNB, K = 500)[1,1]

[1] 5.646496

I hope this clarifies my point a little.

Jonas

messages.body_plain:
Dear Sarah,

of course, the commonsense goodness of fit test (of the type "Do these estimates make sense ?") is the most important of all GoF tests and so if your model didn't pass it, then something is clearly wrong with your combination of data and model. I am not sure what, but I would like to make a couple of comments and have a try at replying to some of your questions at the end of the PDF that you attached. Here they are:

(Sarah's) Main questions
1. How do I choose start values?
+So far nothing I Have tried has worked.
+Also, how many do I need? I have used up to 11, depending on how many are
rendered when coef(whatever model) is run
+I have been choosing my starts=c(values) based on the results from the coef():
2. Is a K value necessary?
+How would I go about chosing those?
+I read that you should start small and go up until it stabilizes but the difference
between no K-value included and K=500 is an increase of 53 detections
3. I ran all null and covariate models with mixture="NB" but that did not change my
results
+When is choosing a mixture necessary? I'm unclear on this.

Some answers:
1. you want to choose inits that are close to the solution (= the parameter estimates). A typical way is to use solutions from a "neighbouring" model, i.e., one that differs, say, by having one fewer covariates. Then you can use the coefficients of that simpler model, but have to add in a zero at the right position as an init for the coefficient of the additional covariate of the new model. That's the basic strategy. You do this step-wise in a progression of ever-more complex models, possibly starting from the simplest model with only the intercept. You need of course exactly as many inits as your model has coefficients and you must put them in the right order

2. K IS NOT A PARAMETER OF THE MODEL. You can think of K as a tuning 'parameter' of the model-fitting procedure, but in principle, it should not affect the results. When it does, then either the default choice of unmarked (max count plus 100) happens to be too low and you have to manually up it and do this repeatedly until the estimates stabilize. Or, and that is the more worrying case, but in principle easily diagnosed: your model may have problems with estimability. This happens especially with NegBin mixtures for the simple binomial mixture model, but perhaps this may also happen with distance sampling models. A K is ALWAYS chosen by default by unmarked, so yes, in this sense, it is always necessary. But it is not always necessary for YOU to change that default choice. If you do change, then you simply increase the value of K, say, from 100 to 250, 500 and 1000. The model run times will increase greatly but at some point you should get identical estimates for two choices of K. If you don't, then you cannot trust your model.

3. The 'mixture' is very much a part of the model, because it is the statistical distribution assumed for the spatial heterogeneity in abundance among sites. You can think of the Negative binomial as a more variable version of a Poisson, thus a more complex mode that we should only use if the simpler model does not fit. You can choose between the two by AIC.

It would be good if you read up on these models to improve your understanding of things like the mixture distribution. This is an essential part of the model.

Hope somebody else has some good ideas with the other problems.

Best regards  --- Marc

> Dear Sarah,
>
> of course, the commonsense goodness of fit test (of the type "Do these estimates make sense ?") is the most important of all GoF tests and so if your model didn't pass it, then something is clearly wrong with your combination of data and model. I am not sure what, but I would like to make a couple of comments and have a try at replying to some of your questions at the end of the PDF that you attached. Here they are:
>
> (Sarah's) Main questions
> 1. How do I choose start values?
> +So far nothing I Have tried has worked.
> +Also, how many do I need? I have used up to 11, depending on how many are
> rendered when coef(whatever model) is run
> +I have been choosing my starts=c(values) based on the results from the coef():
> 2. Is a K value necessary?
> +How would I go about chosing those?
> +I read that you should start small and go up until it stabilizes but the difference
> between no K-value included and K=500 is an increase of 53 detections
> 3. I ran all null and covariate models with mixture="NB" but that did not change my
> results
> +When is choosing a mixture necessary? I'm unclear on this.
>
> Some answers:
> 1. you want to choose inits that are close to the solution (= the parameter estimates). A typical way is to use solutions from a "neighbouring" model, i.e., one that differs, say, by having one fewer covariates. Then you can use the coefficients of that simpler model, but have to add in a zero at the right position as an init for the coefficient of the additional covariate of the new model. That's the basic strategy. You do this step-wise in a progression of ever-more complex models, possibly starting from the simplest model with only the intercept. You need of course exactly as many inits as your model has coefficients and you must put them in the right order
>
> 2. K IS NOT A PARAMETER OF THE MODEL. You can think of K as a tuning 'parameter' of the model-fitting procedure, but in principle, it should not affect the results. When it does, then either the default choice of unmarked (max count plus 100) happens to be too low and you have to manually up it and do this repeatedly until the estimates stabilize. Or, and that is the more worrying case, but in principle easily diagnosed: your model may have problems with estimability. This happens especially with NegBin mixtures for the simple binomial mixture model, but perhaps this may also happen with distance sampling models. A K is ALWAYS chosen by default by unmarked, so yes, in this sense, it is always necessary. But it is not always necessary for YOU to change that default choice. If you do change, then you simply increase the value of K, say, from 100 to 250, 500 and 1000. The model run times will increase greatly but at some point you should get identical estimates for two choices of K. If you don't, then you cannot trust your model.
>
> 3. The 'mixture' is very much a part of the model, because it is the statistical distribution assumed for the spatial heterogeneity in abundance among sites. You can think of the Negative binomial as a more variable version of a Poisson, thus a more complex mode that we should only use if the simpler model does not fit. You can choose between the two by AIC.
>
> It would be good if you read up on these models to improve your understanding of things like the mixture distribution. This is an essential part of the model.
>
> Hope somebody else has some good ideas with the other problems.
>
> Best regards  --- Marc
>

I was expecting the formulation of the detection process in occu() to be a binomial distribution. I understand a Bernoulli distribution is just a binomial distribution with n-trials = 1. So, I guess the function is set up to do either, depending on the formula and data used?

For example, if observation covariates are used, then the Bernoulli distribution is used, and separate estimates of detectability can be estimated for each sampling occasion.  However, if observation covariates are not used, then a binomial distribution is used and one estimate of detectability is estimated for each site?

messages.subject: Re: formulation of detection process in occu()
messages.subject_clean: formulation of detection process in occu()
messages.body_plain:
Hello Cody,

For any given site, the observation data for occu() corresponds to a vector of 0 and 1 representing either or not the species has been detected. In this context, a Bernoulli distribution conditioned on the occupancy status, and the detection probability specific to each site and sampling occasion is applied following:

                         y_ij | z_i ~ Bernoulli(z_i * p_ij)

Technically speaking, the Bernoulli distribution is used regardless, and detection probability will always correspond to the probability of detection the species (given that it's present) on each sampling occasion. If you want to get the overall detection probability (i.e. what it is the probability to detect the species at least once during my sampling on a given site), you'll have to derive this information.

The detection probability can be site specific (p_i), sampling period specific (p_j), neither (p) or both (p_ij), and you are correct, this is going to be determined by the formulation of the model for the observation process (and the corresponding data).

Florent

In your example 'fitted' gives the correct answer, but if we change lam to e.g. 10 and size to 1/5, fitted(fmNB) is no longer equal to exp(coef(fmNB)[1]) * plogis(coef(fmNB)[2]):

> >
> > Now fitted gives:
> >
> > > fitted(fmNB)[1,1]
> > [1] 4.144114
> >
> > but this is not the same as the product of the back transformed coefficients:
> >
> > > exp(coef(fmNB)[1]) * plogis(coef(fmNB)[2])
> > lam(Int)
> > 5.647976
> >
> >

> >

> > [1] 5.646496

> > I hope this clarifies my point a little.

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] RPresence
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I admit that I haven't yet checked out PResence.

However, it seems to be the R version of a Windows program called PRESENCE, which was created originally by Darryl MacKenzie and over the years now mostly by Jim Hines. However, I think that it's fair to say that, yes, unmarked can do quite a bit of occupancy modeling, but PRESENCE has many more occupancy models than does unmarked. For instance, multi-state occupancy models for static and dynamic situations, more false-positive occupancy modeling (I think, dynamic, too) and some slightly spatial models (e.g., the tiger on trails-model of Hines et al. 2010 and I think also a very simple version of an autologistic model, as was used in a recent publication by Yackulik et al). And no doubt quite some more. So I think it's a great thing that one now seems to be able to harness the power of PRESENCE from R, without having to click and point until your fingers hurt.

In terms of the models covered, the main thing where unmarked is 'better' than PRESENCE is in the models for abundance.

Apologies to Jim Hines, Richard Chandler and Ian Fiske for any mis-representation of what both are great pieces of software !

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: can method="L-BFGS-B" be used to fix model covariate coefficient values?
messages.subject_clean: can method="L-BFGS-B" be used to fix model covariate coefficient values?
messages.body_plain:
Say you wanted to fit a model with one large dataset then apply that model to a subset of the original with an additional model covariate. But you do not want the original covariate coefficients to change with the new MLE optimization, which may happen if for example you simply provided the starting values. The L-BFGS-B method allows you to supply upper and lower bounds of each coefficient for the optimization to search within, so I gather typically you would choose a plausible range of values to minimize the processing time spent in unrealistic parameter space. But could you instead choose to set a very narrow range of values to restrict the optimization to the values you got from the original large dataset while then finding the ML solution for the new variable?

Is this a reasonable procedure or will it simply lead to errors because optim doesn't think the model fits the data? What issues would arise from doing this, other than the possibility of the presence of a new variable in the model influencing the other model parameter coefficients and thus potentially ignoring the optimal ML solution for the smaller dataset?
Thanks!
Jay

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] can method="L-BFGS-B" be used to fix model covariate coefficient values?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] can method="L-BFGS-B" be used to fix model covariate coefficient values?
messages.body_plain:
I think that what might be most important for this is to start with the objective you want to achieve rather than starting with describing a set of statistical steps.

Without that objective stated I would say that you're not characterizing maximum likelihood optimization techniques correctly.  If one starts close enough to the maximum likelihood values, the algorithm might not spend any time in unrealistic parameter space.

Also, while convergence might not be achieved with a given set of starting values or convergence takes a lot of time, optim doesn't care about the quality of the fit.  optim simply tries to find the parameter values that maximize the objective function no matter if the data is well-described by the model or not.

So I would start with the standard statistician's question:  What question do you want to answer?

Jim

Maybe I can supply a little more substance than my first response.  This sounds like either the question deals with a variable selection process or a model formulation issue.  If the subset of sites is already known to be different, there's no reason not to build that into the original model such as having two different effects for the additional covariate.  (I would be hesitant to having an effect for that covariate in one subset and no effect in the other unless there was some reasonable/strong justification.)

Jim

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] can method="L-BFGS-B" be used to fix model covariate coefficient values?
messages.body_plain:
Even if you can set the parameters using the upper and lower options for the L-BFGS-B technique, I wouldn't recommend it.  Why?  Mainly because the standard errors (and likely the estimates) of the parameter(s) associated with the added covariate would at best have unknown long-term properties.  I'm reminded of the sentence from Scotty to Captain Kirk:  "I cannae change the laws of physics!".  One who lives by maximum likelihood must die by maximum likelihood.

Now if you could somehow justify a joint prior distribution to perform a Bayesian analysis...but you'd still have to follow the laws of probability.

Jim

But could you instead choose to set a very narrow range of values to restrict the optimization to the values you got from the original large dataset while then finding the ML solution for the new variable?
> > > > >
> > > > > Is this a reasonable procedure or will it simply lead to errors because optim doesn't think the model fits the data? messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am trying to estimate population size on a single 1500m transect (20m width) that has been surveyed on seven occasions during a single season (ultimately, the goal is to compare distance sampling estimates with traditional mark recapture estimates). Originally, I separated the data and ran each occasion separately using distsamp() with a plan to use the survey occasion that produced the highest estimates. To estimate local population size I used parametric bootstrap approach as explained by Chandler (2015).

It seems however, that gdistamp() function might be more appropriate, but I am not sure how to estimate population size (site.level.abundance) after I get lambda (abundance), phi (availability), and p (detection). So far this is what I have:

gyDat<-formatDistData(data,distCol="distance",transectNameCol="transect",occasionCol="occasion",dist.breaks=c(0,2,4,6,8,10))
gumf<-unmarkedFrameGDS(y=as.matrix(gyDat),survey="line",tlength=rep(1500,1),unitsIn="m",numPrimary=7,dist.breaks=c(0,2,4,6,8,10))

g1<-gdistsamp(~1,~1,~1,gumf,output="density",keyfun="halfnorm",unitsOut="ha")

 summary(g1)

Call:

gdistsamp(lambdaformula = ~1, phiformula = ~1, pformula = ~1,

    data = gumf, keyfun = "halfnorm", output = "density", unitsOut = "ha")

Abundance (log-scale):

 Estimate    SE    z   P(>|z|)

     3.76 0.112 33.6 8.09e-248

Availability (logit-scale):

 Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)

    -0.73 0.175 -4.17 2.99e-05

Detection (log-scale):

 Estimate     SE  z  P(>|z|)

     1.56 0.0822 19 2.31e-80

AIC: -224.0016

Number of sites: 1

optim convergence code: 0

optim iterations: 70
Bootstrap iterations: 0

Again, I know how to estimate population size from the model of density with distsamp(), but I am not sure how to do it using the estimates from gdistsamp(). I know that this is probably a simple question but I am having trouble moving forward and conceptualizing getting estimates from gdistsamp() (besides reading that lambda*phi/A in Chandler et al. 2011). Also, any thoughts on running each occasion separately using distsamp()?

Thank you so much for your time.
Ivana

As traditionally performed, the N-mixture assumes that N is constant at a specific site for all occasions. I provided a reproducible example using the Island Scrub Jay data and example code from the package with a few tweaks.

However when I use the linearComb function and backtransform the prediction I get the expected results.  Is there a way to get the predictions and standard errors scaled correctly with the predict function using an offset in the model?

covs <- scale(issj[,c("elevation", "forest", "chaparral")])
area <- pi*300^2 / 10000

                            siteCovs=data.frame(covs, area),
                            dist.breaks=c(0,100,200,300), unitsIn="m", survey="point")
## This model has an offset

                jayumf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="abund",

## This model doesn't have an offset

Richard

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Offset in distsamp model predictions
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Offset in distsamp model predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

I think the predictions are correct. In the model without the offset, lambda is defined as the expected number of individuals at a site. Since all sites had an area of 28.27, this is the expected number of individuals in an area of 28.27 ha. In the model with the offset, lambda is defined as the expected number of individuals per unit area. If you predict from this model using area=28.27ha is should give you the same result as the model without the offset, which implicitly assumes that area=28.27. The two models should only yield different results if you change "area" to something other than 28.27 when making your predictions.

To correctly use linearComb() when an area offset is preset, you need to multiply the back-transformed result by the area of interest. However, it's easier to use predict().

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

I was suggesting that you fit the model with the correct area (28.27 ha) and then explore the effects of changing area when making predictions. If you use the same area for fitting and predicting, you will get the same predicted abundance as you would from a model without the offset.

The predict function is just evaluating the log-linear model, which looks like this (for a single covariate):

E(N) = lambda = exp(beta0 + beta1*x + log(area))

which is the same as

E(N) = lambda = exp(beta0 + beta1*x)*area

If you fit a model without the offset, you will notice that the intercept changes, but the predictions of E(N) will be the same if you use the same offset as was used to fit the model.

Richard

messages.subject: "Fitted" values for unmarked Occu - Does it estimate occupancy based on detection history?
messages.subject_clean: "Fitted" values for unmarked Occu - Does it estimate occupancy based on detection history?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

The short version: what exactly is the "matrix of expected values" returned by "fitted" from an unmarkedOccuFrame?

Shockingly naive question, but I've been unable to find a satisfactory answer in the package guide or elsewhere on this forum, any help appreciated!

The longer version:

I have camera trap data with both site and observation level covariates for detection, and site covariates for occupancy (although not all are included in all models, I performed model ranking to determine relevant covariates).

I would like a single value, for each camera site, estimating a probability of occupancy based on it's covariates and the detection history at that site, and detection probabilities from other site's histories to account for imperfect detection. Is this what the code "fitted(fm)" will delivery? My output varies by each day, I'm imagining as a result of the daily detection covariate, but are these values actually occupancy? I have seen mention elsewhere of aggregating across fitted values (for bootstrapping, etc) and am curious if that is the approach to take here?

I was not using the Predict function because I am not trying to estimate what occupancy would be under certain set circumstances, rather for each site with the observed data.

If there is an obvious line in the documentation I am missing my apologies, or if you can direct me to read something elsewhere I would value it very much!

Thanks,
Bryn

messages.body_plain:
hi Bryn,

 The fitted values are E(y_{ij}) = p_{ij}*psi_{I}  (i.e., the combined product of detection and occupancy)

 From your description I think what you want is an estimate of E(z_{I} | data at site i) which can be obtained from the ranef function (see p. 569 in the Kery and Royle AHM book).

 There is considerable guidance on goodness-of-fit in these models starting on page 589 of the AHM book...

regards,
andy
